summary: Children learn the body's 'levels of organisation' as a nested hierarchy of increasing scale: tiny cells (too small to see without a microscope) are the building blocks; groups of similar cells form tissues; different tissues combine into organs (heart, stomach, lungs); and organs working together form organ systems (the circulatory system). The learning is carried by a sense of scale (the body has trillions of cells) and by tracing ONE concrete example through all four levels (muscle cell → muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system), zooming both in and out rather than defining four abstract words. A central aim is to confront the intuition that organs are made of solid 'stuff' rather than of cells.
misconceptions: 'Organs are made of solid stuff/material, not cells' — missing that every organ is built from cells and tissues.
'Cells, tissues and organs are the same size / roughly similar' — missing the huge scale difference across levels.
'Tissue means a paper tissue / kitchen roll' — the everyday word interfering with the biological meaning (a group of similar cells).
'The body has just a few cells' — rather than trillions, too small to see individually.
'An organ system is a single organ' — missing that a system is several organs working together.
'Cells are only in some parts of the body' — rather than everywhere, as the universal building block.

activities.title: Zoom along one example: body to cell and back
steps: Start by looking at the whole body, then move into the circulatory system, then to the heart, then into muscle tissue, then into a single muscle cell shown as if under a microscope.
At each level, name the level and say how it relates to the level above and below it (e.g. 'muscle tissue is made of many muscle cells and forms part of the heart').
Reverse the journey, zooming OUT from a single muscle cell up to the whole circulatory system, so the levels are seen to nest and combine both ways.
Use a 'how many cells in your body?' reveal to land the idea that the body has trillions of cells, each too small to see without a microscope.
State in your own words that the heart is not made of 'special heart stuff' but is built from tissue, which is built from billions of tiny cells.
activities.insight: The four levels (cell → tissue → organ → organ system) form a nested hierarchy of increasing scale; a familiar organ like the heart is ultimately built from billions of tiny cells.

activities.title: Build it up: assemble the levels and place new examples
steps: Combine many similar cells to form a tissue, several tissues to build an organ, and several organs into an organ system, so the COMBINE direction is seen explicitly, and note that an organ system is several organs working together, not a single organ.
Take a new example (a nerve cell, the stomach, blood, skin) and place it at the correct level on the ladder.
For a chosen organ, build the chain yourself: e.g. for the stomach or lungs, say which cells form which tissue, which tissue forms the organ, and which system the organ belongs to.
Decide whether a part of the body (such as skin or bone) is made of cells, and justify your answer.
activities.insight: Each level is built by combining many of the level below, an organ system is several organs working together, and any body part — not just blood — can be placed on the ladder and traced back to cells.

activities.title: Consolidation and diagnostic check
steps: Order the four levels from smallest to biggest: cell → tissue → organ → organ system.
Categorise a set of examples (nerve cell, stomach, blood, circulatory system) by their level.

Answer the diagnostic: 'Your heart is an organ. If you looked at it closer and closer with a stronger and stronger microscope, what is it actually made of? Put organ, cell, tissue, organ system in order from smallest to biggest, and explain how each one is built from the one before it.'
Extend to a probe: make the same build-up chain for the stomach or the lungs; explain why you can't see a single cell just by looking closely; say whether skin is made of cells too.
activities.insight: A full understanding both orders the levels correctly AND explains how each level is built from the one below, transferable to a new organ.

checkQuestion: Your heart is an organ. If you looked at it closer and closer with a stronger and stronger microscope, what is it actually MADE of? Put these in order from smallest to biggest — organ, cell, tissue, organ system — and explain how each one is built from the one before it.
checkAnswer: From smallest to biggest: cell → tissue → organ → organ system. Cells are the tiny building blocks (too small to see without a microscope); many similar cells together make a tissue (muscle cells make muscle tissue); different tissues together make an organ (muscle and other tissues make the heart); and organs working together make an organ system (the heart with the blood vessels makes the circulatory system). So the heart is ultimately made of billions of tiny cells.
